title: The Dominant Student
displayTitle: How do you handle Maria?
instruction: Choose the response that best reflects senior EFL teaching practice.

_items.text: Thank Maria for her contribution, then use a structured turn-taking technique: assign each student a number and have them build a collaborative story one sentence at a time. Maria speaks when it's her turn, just like everyone else.
_items._feedback: Excellent. You redirected Maria's energy into a structured, equitable activity. Numbered turn-taking builds classroom community and ensures every voice is heard — without embarrassing the dominant speaker.

_items.text: Interrupt Maria politely, say 'interesting, let's hear what others think,' and cold-call three quiet students in a row. If they struggle, bridge with scaffolding questions.
_items._feedback: Your intent is right, but cold-calling anxious learners can increase their affective filter. A structured technique — like numbered sentences or timed pair-shares — is less threatening and more inclusive.

_items.text: Let Maria finish — her story is engaging and entertaining the class. Use her narrative as a springboard for the next activity and encourage others to share examples from their own travels.
_items._feedback: Letting one student dominate 5+ minutes of a 90-minute lesson sends a signal that airtime is unequal. The quieter learners in the back already disengaged. Senior teachers establish equitable turn-taking from the first minute.

_feedback.title: Feedback
_feedback.correct: Structured turn-taking is a hallmark of experienced teaching. It maintains motivation across all learners and prevents the 'Dominant Student Trap' — one of the most common classroom management challenges in EFL.
_feedback._correct: Structured turn-taking is a hallmark of experienced teaching. It maintains motivation across all learners and prevents the 'Dominant Student Trap' — one of the most common classroom management challenges in EFL.

_incorrect.notFinal: The key principle is equitable airtime without public embarrassment. Structured techniques like numbered turn-taking or timed pair-shares work better than interrupting or letting one learner dominate.
_incorrect.final: The key principle is equitable airtime without public embarrassment. Structured techniques like numbered turn-taking or timed pair-shares work better than interrupting or letting one learner dominate.

title: Error Correction Dilemma
displayTitle: When do you correct?
instruction: Choose the approach that best supports both fluency development and accuracy improvement.

_items.text: Let the discussion flow uninterrupted. Note the 3 systematic errors on the board discreetly. After the fluency stage ends, write the errors on the board and ask the class to identify and correct them collaboratively in a 'grammar detective' slot.
_items._feedback: This is the 'delayed correction' approach — best practice for fluency stages. You preserved the communicative flow, then used learner-generated errors for a focused, memorable correction slot. The collaborative 'detective' format keeps ego out of it.

_items.text: Gently recast each error on the spot — respond to the student naturally by repeating their sentence correctly: 'Ah, you will go to university next year? Great! And what will you study?' without explicitly pointing out the mistake.
_items._feedback: Recasting is common and well-intentioned, but research (Lyster & Ranta, 1997) shows it's the least effective correction technique — learners often don't notice it. Delayed, explicit correction has higher uptake rates.

_items.text: Stop the activity after the first few errors. Drill each corrected form chorally and individually before allowing the discussion to resume. Accuracy builds on a foundation of correct habit formation.
_items._feedback: Interrupting a fluency activity for drilling undermines its purpose. Learners need to develop the ability to communicate despite imperfect grammar. Schedule accuracy work for the controlled practice stage, not during free production.

_feedback.title: Feedback
_feedback.correct: You distinguished between fluency and accuracy stages — a core skill senior teachers master. Delayed correction during post-activity feedback slots is backed by decades of SLA research (Ellis, 2009; Lyster, Saito & Sato, 2013).
_feedback._correct: You distinguished between fluency and accuracy stages — a core skill senior teachers master. Delayed correction during post-activity feedback slots is backed by decades of SLA research (Ellis, 2009; Lyster, Saito & Sato, 2013).

_incorrect.notFinal: During fluency activities, the goal is communication, not perfect accuracy. Delayed correction — noting errors during the activity and addressing them post-task — is the research-backed approach for this stage.
_incorrect.final: During fluency activities, the goal is communication, not perfect accuracy. Delayed correction — noting errors during the activity and addressing them post-task — is the research-backed approach for this stage.

title: Methodology Fork
displayTitle: Which approach for a mixed-purpose B2 class?
instruction: Choose the methodology that best serves this diverse group of learners.

_items.text: Task-Based Language Teaching (TBLT): Start with a communicative task — a 5-minute mini-debate on a controversial topic. Let learners struggle with the language they have. Then focus on form: extract and practise the functional exponents for opinion-giving that emerged from their attempt.
_items._feedback: TBLT is ideal for mixed-purpose groups. It's inherently communicative (IELTS students get speaking practice), task-relevant (business professionals use real-world language), and engaging (retired learners enjoy the debate). The 'task → focus on form' sequence mirrors how natural language acquisition works.

_items.text: Presentation-Practice-Production (PPP): Present a list of useful phrases for opinion-giving ("In my view...", "It could be argued that..."), drill them chorally, then have students complete a controlled gap-fill before moving to a freer discussion.
_items._feedback: PPP is reliable and well-structured, but it's teacher-centred and assumes all learners need the same language items. For a diverse group, TBLT's 'needs-driven' approach — where language emerges from the task — is more responsive to varied learner goals.

_items.text: Grammar-Translation: Present the rules for concession clauses and contrastive linking phrases on the board. Have students translate 10 sentences from their L1 into English using the target structures. If time remains, open for discussion.
_items._feedback: Grammar-Translation has limited application in modern communicative classrooms. At B2 level, learners need functional language use, not metallinguistic rule explanation. Translation may help, but as a primary methodology it fails to develop speaking fluency.

_feedback.title: Feedback
_feedback.correct: TBLT is widely considered the most effective approach for mixed-purpose, communicative classes (Willis & Willis, 2007; Ellis, 2003). It prioritises meaningful use, then provides just-in-time language support based on learner needs.
_feedback._correct: TBLT is widely considered the most effective approach for mixed-purpose, communicative classes (Willis & Willis, 2007; Ellis, 2003). It prioritises meaningful use, then provides just-in-time language support based on learner needs.

_incorrect.notFinal: For a mixed-purpose Upper-Intermediate group, TBLT offers the flexibility to address varied learner goals within a single communicative framework. PPP is systematic but less responsive to emergent needs.
_incorrect.final: For a mixed-purpose Upper-Intermediate group, TBLT offers the flexibility to address varied learner goals within a single communicative framework. PPP is systematic but less responsive to emergent needs.

title: The Wrong Answer
displayTitle: How do you correct Ahmed?
instruction: Choose the approach that corrects the error while protecting Ahmed's confidence.

_items.text: Acknowledge Ahmed's attempt with a nod, then ask a Concept Checking Question (CCQ) that guides him to self-correct: 'Good try — is it she have or she has? Think about the subject.' If he self-corrects, praise the effort and move on.
_items._feedback: A CCQ that prompts self-correction is the gold standard here. It engages Ahmed in noticing his own error (noticing hypothesis, Schmidt, 1990) — which leads to deeper acquisition than being told the answer. And it preserves his dignity by letting him 'find' the correction himself.

_items.text: Gently correct: 'She has visited three countries. Repeat after me, Ahmed: She has visited.' Then move to the next item on the page so he doesn't dwell on the mistake.
_items._feedback: While moving on quickly spares some embarrassment, providing the correction does not activate the learner's own processing. Self-correction — guided by a CCQ — leads to better long-term retention and builds learner autonomy.

_items.text: Make a note of the error and address it with the whole class during the feedback plenary: 'I noticed some of you said she have — remember, we need she has. Ahmed, can you give us the correct sentence?'
_items._feedback: Public attention — even in a feedback slot — can heighten anxiety for a confidence-sensitive learner. A private CCQ or a quiet one-to-one prompt during monitoring is more face-saving. Reserve whole-class feedback for anonymous, board-based correction.

_feedback.title: Feedback
_feedback.correct: Self-correction via CCQ is a sophisticated teaching move. It reduces the affective filter (Krashen, 1982), promotes noticing (Schmidt, 1990), and maintains rapport. Experienced teachers use it as their default correction technique in controlled practice.
_feedback._correct: Self-correction via CCQ is a sophisticated teaching move. It reduces the affective filter (Krashen, 1982), promotes noticing (Schmidt, 1990), and maintains rapport. Experienced teachers use it as their default correction technique in controlled practice.

_incorrect.notFinal: For confidence-sensitive learners, gentle CCQs that prompt self-correction are more effective than direct correction or public attention. The learner corrects themselves, which builds both accuracy and confidence.
_incorrect.final: For confidence-sensitive learners, gentle CCQs that prompt self-correction are more effective than direct correction or public attention. The learner corrects themselves, which builds both accuracy and confidence.

title: The Challenge
displayTitle: How do you handle Pablo?
instruction: Choose the response that best manages this challenge while protecting the class dynamic.

_items.text: Acknowledge his concern calmly: 'I hear you, Pablo. Pair work can feel different from what you're used to. Here's why I use it: research shows you learn more when you practise speaking actively rather than listening to me talk. Try this task for 5 minutes, and if you still find it unhelpful, we can chat during the break.' Then direct the class back to the activity.
_items._feedback: You validated his concern without surrendering classroom leadership. The 'try it for 5 minutes' technique is a micro-commitment strategy — it lowers resistance by reducing the perceived cost of participation. You built rapport while maintaining authority.

_items.text: Explain firmly that communicative activities are part of the curriculum and that while he is entitled to his opinion, the class will proceed as planned. Offer to discuss his concerns after class, then return to the activity without further delay.
_items._feedback: Your firmness is understandable, but dismissing his concern publicly without validation can entrench resistance. A brief acknowledgement before pivoting — rather than a firm 'this is the rule' — preserves more rapport.

_items.text: Ask Pablo what he would prefer to do instead. If he can suggest a valid alternative, incorporate it. If he can't, say 'let's try the activity and review it together at the end — you might be surprised.'
_items._feedback: Asking what he'd prefer is a reasonable negotiation tactic, but it risks ceding too much control to one learner in front of the class. Other students may interpret this as the teacher being unsure. A brief acknowledgement + micro-commitment is a stronger position.

_feedback.title: Feedback
_feedback.correct: This is the 'validate + redirect' technique — one of the most effective de-escalation strategies for resistant learners. You maintained authority, acknowledged the learner's perspective, and used a micro-commitment to keep the lesson moving. The post-lesson chat creates a safe space for deeper conversation.
_feedback._correct: This is the 'validate + redirect' technique — one of the most effective de-escalation strategies for resistant learners. You maintained authority, acknowledged the learner's perspective, and used a micro-commitment to keep the lesson moving. The post-lesson chat creates a safe space for deeper conversation.

_incorrect.notFinal: The most effective approach for a public challenge is validate-then-redirect: acknowledge the concern briefly, explain your reasoning (evidence-based), and use a low-risk commitment ('try this for 5 minutes') to bring the learner back in.
_incorrect.final: The most effective approach for a public challenge is validate-then-redirect: acknowledge the concern briefly, explain your reasoning (evidence-based), and use a low-risk commitment ('try this for 5 minutes') to bring the learner back in.

title: Scenario Complete
displayTitle: Reflection & Growth
body:
Congratulations. You have completed EFL Classroom Dilemmas: Senior Teaching Decisions.

What You Navigated

This scenario reflected five of the most common — and most complex — situations senior EFL teachers face:

  1. The Dominant Student — Managing equitable airtime without public embarrassment
  2. Error Correction — Choosing when and how to correct during fluency stages
  3. Methodology Selection — Matching your approach to a mixed-purpose group
  4. Face-Saving Feedback — Correcting errors while protecting learner confidence
  5. Student Resistance — De-escalating public challenges without losing authority

Key Research Principles

  • Affective Filter (Krashen, 1982): Anxiety blocks acquisition. Every decision that lowers a learner's anxiety — equitable turn-taking, delayed correction, CCQs, validation — creates better conditions for learning.
  • Noticing Hypothesis (Schmidt, 1990): Learners must notice their own errors to acquire the correct form. Self-correction via CCQ is more effective than teacher-provided correction.
  • Task-Based Learning (Willis & Willis, 2007): Real communication tasks + just-in-time language support produce more robust acquisition than presentation-led approaches.
  • Corrective Feedback (Lyster & Ranta, 1997): Delayed explicit correction has highest uptake; recasts have lowest. Choose your correction strategy based on the stage of the lesson.

Your Teaching Philosophy

The choices you made reflect your teaching values. Did you prioritise equity? Fluency? Learner confidence? Classroom authority? There is no single 'right' path through this scenario — experienced teachers make context-sensitive decisions based on their learners, their setting, and their principles.

What matters is that every decision was intentional — grounded in research and tailored to the moment.

— End of Scenario —

title: Managing Multi-Level Classes
displayTitle: What is the BEST approach for this multi-level Elementary class?

_items.text: Differentiate by providing extension tasks for the stronger pair and scaffolded support for the beginners, while keeping the core lesson on Daily Routines.
_items._feedback: Correct! Well reasoned.

_items.text: Stick rigidly to the coursebook — the syllabus says Unit 4, so teach Unit 4 at the same pace for everyone.
_items._feedback: Not the best choice. Review the scenario for the most appropriate response.

_items.text: Abandon the coursebook entirely and design a completely new lesson on the spot.
_items._feedback: Not the best choice. Review the scenario for the most appropriate response.

_items.text: Move the stronger learners to a higher class and let the beginners catch up on their own.
_items._feedback: Not the best choice. Review the scenario for the most appropriate response.

_feedback.title: Explanation
_feedback.correct: Differentiation is the professional response: keep the core content but adjust the level of support. The stronger pair can be extended, while beginners get scaffolding. Abandoning the syllabus or moving students ignores DoS constraints and learner needs.

_incorrect.final: Differentiation is the professional response: keep the core content but adjust the level of support. The stronger pair can be extended, while beginners get scaffolding. Abandoning the syllabus or moving students ignores DoS constraints and learner needs.

_feedback._notFinal: Differentiation is the professional response: keep the core content but adjust the level of support. The stronger pair can be extended, while beginners get scaffolding. Abandoning the syllabus or moving students ignores DoS constraints and learner needs.

title: AI-Generated Homework
displayTitle: What is the MOST professional response to Elena's ChatGPT-generated homework?

_items.text: Speak to Elena privately: acknowledge her effort, explain why AI homework undermines her learning, and agree on a way forward — such as in-class writing tasks that she completes without AI.
_items._feedback: Correct! Well reasoned.

_items.text: Ignore it — other teachers said to, and there is no specific AI policy.
_items._feedback: Not the best choice. Review the scenario for the most appropriate response.

_items.text: Report Elena to the DoS immediately for academic dishonesty.
_items._feedback: Not the best choice. Review the scenario for the most appropriate response.

_items.text: Publicly warn the whole class that AI-detection software will be used.
_items._feedback: Not the best choice. Review the scenario for the most appropriate response.

_feedback.title: Explanation
_feedback.correct: A private, respectful conversation addresses the issue directly without humiliating Elena. It treats her as a person, not a policy violation. Ignoring it normalises the behaviour; escalating without discussion damages trust.

_incorrect.final: A private, respectful conversation addresses the issue directly without humiliating Elena. It treats her as a person, not a policy violation. Ignoring it normalises the behaviour; escalating without discussion damages trust.

_feedback._notFinal: A private, respectful conversation addresses the issue directly without humiliating Elena. It treats her as a person, not a policy violation. Ignoring it normalises the behaviour; escalating without discussion damages trust.

title: The Speaking Gap
displayTitle: What is the root cause of Mei's problem?

_items.text: Mei has developed strong receptive and test-taking skills but lacks communicative practice — her learning has been assessment-focused, not use-focused.
_items._feedback: Correct! Well reasoned.

_items.text: Mei is lazy and hasn't been practising speaking outside of class.
_items._feedback: Not the best choice. Review the scenario for the most appropriate response.

_items.text: The coursebook is too difficult for her level.
_items._feedback: Not the best choice. Review the scenario for the most appropriate response.

_items.text: Mei has a language learning disability that prevents her from speaking.
_items._feedback: Not the best choice. Review the scenario for the most appropriate response.

_feedback.title: Explanation
_feedback.correct: Mei's high test scores show she has learned the rules — but she has never transferred that knowledge to real communication. This is a classic 'assessment gap': we test what's easy to measure, not what matters most.

_incorrect.final: Mei's high test scores show she has learned the rules — but she has never transferred that knowledge to real communication. This is a classic 'assessment gap': we test what's easy to measure, not what matters most.

_feedback._notFinal: Mei's high test scores show she has learned the rules — but she has never transferred that knowledge to real communication. This is a classic 'assessment gap': we test what's easy to measure, not what matters most.

title: ADHD in the Classroom
displayTitle: Which immediate adjustment BEST supports Diego while respecting the other learners?

_items.text: Chunk the reading task into smaller steps: give Diego the first 2 paragraphs to read, then check comprehension before moving on — and let him stand or use a fidget tool while reading.
_items._feedback: Correct! Well reasoned.

_items.text: Send Diego to the DoS's office — he's disrupting the adults.
_items._feedback: Not the best choice. Review the scenario for the most appropriate response.

_items.text: Ignore the behaviour and keep teaching — he will eventually settle down.
_items._feedback: Not the best choice. Review the scenario for the most appropriate response.

_items.text: Give Diego all 8 questions at once and tell him to finish quickly so he can leave early.
_items._feedback: Not the best choice. Review the scenario for the most appropriate response.

_feedback.title: Explanation
_feedback.correct: Chunking tasks, allowing movement, and permitting fidget tools are research-backed ADHD accommodations. They support Diego without reducing expectations or disrupting others. Sending him out or ignoring the problem are not professional solutions.

_incorrect.final: Chunking tasks, allowing movement, and permitting fidget tools are research-backed ADHD accommodations. They support Diego without reducing expectations or disrupting others. Sending him out or ignoring the problem are not professional solutions.

_feedback._notFinal: Chunking tasks, allowing movement, and permitting fidget tools are research-backed ADHD accommodations. They support Diego without reducing expectations or disrupting others. Sending him out or ignoring the problem are not professional solutions.

title: Adapt or Follow the Book?
displayTitle: Should you invest the extra 2 hours to localise the lesson?

_items.text: Yes — localising the material connects learning to learners' lives, which research shows increases engagement and retention. The 2 hours is an investment in deeper learning.
_items._feedback: Correct! Well reasoned.

_items.text: No — the coursebook is approved material and following it protects you if the lesson goes badly.
_items._feedback: Not the best choice. Review the scenario for the most appropriate response.

_items.text: No — learners don't care about the environment anyway.
_items._feedback: Not the best choice. Review the scenario for the most appropriate response.

_items.text: Yes — but only if you can reuse the materials for future classes, otherwise it's a waste of time.
_items._feedback: Not the best choice. Review the scenario for the most appropriate response.

_feedback.title: Explanation
_feedback.correct: Localisation demonstrates responsive teaching — meeting learners where they are. While it requires time, the pedagogical benefit of connecting content to learners' real-world context is well established.

_incorrect.final: Localisation demonstrates responsive teaching — meeting learners where they are. While it requires time, the pedagogical benefit of connecting content to learners' real-world context is well established.

_feedback._notFinal: Localisation demonstrates responsive teaching — meeting learners where they are. While it requires time, the pedagogical benefit of connecting content to learners' real-world context is well established.

title: Standardised Marking Dilemma
displayTitle: How should you score Anna's speaking test performance?

_items.text: Score holistically: 4/5 for Fluency (confident, clear), 4/5 for Lexical Resource (wide range), 3/5 for Accuracy (6 errors). The overall communicative effectiveness outweighs the grammatical inaccuracies.
_items._feedback: Correct! Well reasoned.

_items.text: Give 3/5 across all criteria — errors are errors, and standardisation means consistency above all.
_items._feedback: Not the best choice. Review the scenario for the most appropriate response.

_items.text: Give 5/5 across the board — she communicated well and that's what matters.
_items._feedback: Not the best choice. Review the scenario for the most appropriate response.

_items.text: Fail her — she made grammatical errors at Pre-Intermediate level.
_items._feedback: Not the best choice. Review the scenario for the most appropriate response.

_feedback.title: Explanation
_feedback.correct: Holistic scoring that balances criteria reflects the complexity of real communication. Anna's strengths in fluency and range outweigh her accuracy errors, which are developmental. Rigid error-counting ignores communicative competence.

_incorrect.final: Holistic scoring that balances criteria reflects the complexity of real communication. Anna's strengths in fluency and range outweigh her accuracy errors, which are developmental. Rigid error-counting ignores communicative competence.

_feedback._notFinal: Holistic scoring that balances criteria reflects the complexity of real communication. Anna's strengths in fluency and range outweigh her accuracy errors, which are developmental. Rigid error-counting ignores communicative competence.

title: Error Correction Timing
displayTitle: What's the BEST response to the conditional error pattern?

_items.text: Pause the lesson, do a 3-minute clarification board-work on the target form (If + past simple, would + base), then let learners who are ready move to freer practice while those who need more support do a controlled practice worksheet.
_items._feedback: Correct! Well reasoned.

_items.text: Ignore the errors — fluency is the aim, and correction can come next lesson.
_items._feedback: Not the best choice. Review the scenario for the most appropriate response.

_items.text: Have the whole class do an extra 10 gap-fill exercises before anyone moves on.
_items._feedback: Not the best choice. Review the scenario for the most appropriate response.

_items.text: Tell students to remember the rule for homework and move on.
_items._feedback: Not the best choice. Review the scenario for the most appropriate response.

_feedback.title: Explanation
_feedback.correct: A brief clarification addresses the error at the point of need without derailing the lesson goals. Splitting the class lets those ready for freer practice proceed while others get targeted support — differentiation in action.

_incorrect.final: A brief clarification addresses the error at the point of need without derailing the lesson goals. Splitting the class lets those ready for freer practice proceed while others get targeted support — differentiation in action.

_feedback._notFinal: A brief clarification addresses the error at the point of need without derailing the lesson goals. Splitting the class lets those ready for freer practice proceed while others get targeted support — differentiation in action.

title: Honouring Learner Preferences
displayTitle: How do you reconcile Klaus's explicit preferences with your professional knowledge?

_items.text: Acknowledge Klaus's preferences and explain your rationale: 'I will teach the grammar and vocabulary you want, but I will also gradually introduce short speaking tasks so you can see the benefit. Let's try one together first.'
_items._feedback: Correct! Well reasoned.

_items.text: Do exactly what Klaus asks — grammar and technical articles only. The client is always right.
_items._feedback: Not the best choice. Review the scenario for the most appropriate response.

_items.text: Tell Klaus his preferences are wrong and communicative methods are superior.
_items._feedback: Not the best choice. Review the scenario for the most appropriate response.

_items.text: Refuse the client and recommend a different teacher.
_items._feedback: Not the best choice. Review the scenario for the most appropriate response.

_feedback.title: Explanation
_feedback.correct: The professional middle ground: honour the learner's stated needs while gently expanding their comfort zone. Explaining the 'why' builds trust and buy-in. Dismissing preferences damages the relationship.

_incorrect.final: The professional middle ground: honour the learner's stated needs while gently expanding their comfort zone. Explaining the 'why' builds trust and buy-in. Dismissing preferences damages the relationship.

_feedback._notFinal: The professional middle ground: honour the learner's stated needs while gently expanding their comfort zone. Explaining the 'why' builds trust and buy-in. Dismissing preferences damages the relationship.

title: Teaching to the Test?
displayTitle: How do you prepare your learners for a standardised exam without abandoning your communicative principles?

_items.text: Continue communicative lessons as usual, then add 15 minutes of exam familiarisation per lesson in the final 3 weeks — focusing on test strategies, not teaching to the test.
_items._feedback: Correct! Well reasoned.

_items.text: Abandon communicative activities and drill past exam papers for the last month — passing is what matters.
_items._feedback: Not the best choice. Review the scenario for the most appropriate response.

_items.text: Complain to the DoS that the exam doesn't align with your teaching philosophy and refuse to prepare learners for it.
_items._feedback: Not the best choice. Review the scenario for the most appropriate response.

_items.text: Tell learners not to worry about the exam — their fluency will carry them through.
_items._feedback: Not the best choice. Review the scenario for the most appropriate response.

_feedback.title: Explanation
_feedback.correct: Ethical exam preparation balances maintaining good teaching with strategic familiarisation. Brief, targeted test-prep in the final weeks gives learners the best of both worlds: real proficiency + exam confidence.

_incorrect.final: Ethical exam preparation balances maintaining good teaching with strategic familiarisation. Brief, targeted test-prep in the final weeks gives learners the best of both worlds: real proficiency + exam confidence.

_feedback._notFinal: Ethical exam preparation balances maintaining good teaching with strategic familiarisation. Brief, targeted test-prep in the final weeks gives learners the best of both worlds: real proficiency + exam confidence.

title: Safeguarding or Overreaction?
displayTitle: What is your MOST appropriate response to Yuki's essay?

_items.text: Provide written feedback on the writing quality as usual, but in the next one-to-one, gently ask: 'I noticed your essay mentions a hotel room meeting — how did that make you feel at the time?' This opens a door without forcing it.
_items._feedback: Correct! Well reasoned.

_items.text: Ignore the sentence — it's probably nothing and you don't want to cause trouble.
_items._feedback: Not the best choice. Review the scenario for the most appropriate response.

_items.text: Report Yuki to safeguarding immediately without speaking to her first.
_items._feedback: Not the best choice. Review the scenario for the most appropriate response.

_items.text: Write 'This sentence concerns me' in red pen on her essay.
_items._feedback: Not the best choice. Review the scenario for the most appropriate response.

_feedback.title: Explanation
_feedback.correct: Teaching involves pastoral care. Acknowledging possible disclosure with sensitivity — giving the learner control over whether to share more — is the professional balance between ignoring a potential issue and overreacting. Written margin comments about concerns can be distressing.

_incorrect.final: Teaching involves pastoral care. Acknowledging possible disclosure with sensitivity — giving the learner control over whether to share more — is the professional balance between ignoring a potential issue and overreacting. Written margin comments about concerns can be distressing.

_feedback._notFinal: Teaching involves pastoral care. Acknowledging possible disclosure with sensitivity — giving the learner control over whether to share more — is the professional balance between ignoring a potential issue and overreacting. Written margin comments about concerns can be distressing.

title: Professional Boundaries
displayTitle: What is the MOST professional response to Carlos's request?

_items.text: Thank Carlos for his dedication and explain that you use a professional channel instead: 'Please email me or ask questions in the class group chat on our learning platform. I will respond within 24 hours.'
_items._feedback: Correct! Well reasoned.

_items.text: Share your number — Carlos said it's just for homework and he seems trustworthy.
_items._feedback: Not the best choice. Review the scenario for the most appropriate response.

_items.text: Say no without explanation — it's none of his business why.
_items._feedback: Not the best choice. Review the scenario for the most appropriate response.

_items.text: Create a WhatsApp group for the whole class — that solves the boundary issue.
_items._feedback: Not the best choice. Review the scenario for the most appropriate response.

_feedback.title: Explanation
_feedback.correct: Professional boundaries protect both teacher and learner. Offering a clear alternative (email / platform) maintains supportiveness without crossing the line. A class WhatsApp group can blur boundaries further and create expectation of 24/7 availability.

_incorrect.final: Professional boundaries protect both teacher and learner. Offering a clear alternative (email / platform) maintains supportiveness without crossing the line. A class WhatsApp group can blur boundaries further and create expectation of 24/7 availability.

_feedback._notFinal: Professional boundaries protect both teacher and learner. Offering a clear alternative (email / platform) maintains supportiveness without crossing the line. A class WhatsApp group can blur boundaries further and create expectation of 24/7 availability.

title: L1 Use in Class
displayTitle: How should you respond to Fatima's explanation about using her L1?

_items.text: Acknowledge her reasoning: 'I understand — sometimes thinking in your own language first helps. Let's agree: you can use L1 to clarify instructions with your partner, but then share your answer in English. Does that work?'
_items._feedback: Correct! Well reasoned.

_items.text: Strictly enforce English-only — the policy is the policy.
_items._feedback: Not the best choice. Review the scenario for the most appropriate response.

_items.text: Tell Fatima she should be able to think in English by now.
_items._feedback: Not the best choice. Review the scenario for the most appropriate response.

_items.text: Allow unlimited L1 use — if it helps understanding, it's fine.
_items._feedback: Not the best choice. Review the scenario for the most appropriate response.

_feedback.title: Explanation
_feedback.correct: Judicious L1 use is supported by SLA research — it can aid cognitive processing without hindering acquisition. A negotiated compromise respects the learner's cognitive process while maintaining the English-speaking classroom environment.

_incorrect.final: Judicious L1 use is supported by SLA research — it can aid cognitive processing without hindering acquisition. A negotiated compromise respects the learner's cognitive process while maintaining the English-speaking classroom environment.

_feedback._notFinal: Judicious L1 use is supported by SLA research — it can aid cognitive processing without hindering acquisition. A negotiated compromise respects the learner's cognitive process while maintaining the English-speaking classroom environment.

title: Demo Lesson Dilemma
displayTitle: What should you do about the 7-year-old demonstration lesson?

_items.text: Be honest with your DoS: explain your lack of YL experience and offer to co-teach with an experienced YL teacher, or observe one first and then do the demo.
_items._feedback: Correct! Well reasoned.

_items.text: Accept the lesson and figure it out on the day — you can't say no to your DoS.

title: Course Complete
displayTitle: Course Complete
body:
You've Completed All 20 Dilemmas!

You've navigated a full term of real-world EFL teaching dilemmas — from the dominant student in Week 1 to the reflective teacher in Week 10. Each decision you made reflects your professional judgment and teaching philosophy.

Your Teaching Philosophy

The choices you made reflect a practice rooted in equity, empathy, evidence, and adaptability.

Teaching is not about being perfect — it's about being present, reflective, and willing to grow. Every dilemma you faced is an opportunity to become the teacher your learners deserve.

You can restart the course at any time from the menu.
